papers.title: EasyFoam: Skill-Oriented OpenFOAM Agents with Evidence-Driven Evolution
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

papers.title: Enhancing Resolution and Reliability with Attention Mechanisms in Nuclear Accident Surrogate Modeling
papers.abstract: Severe accident (SA) analysis of nuclear power plants relies on system codes such as MAAP, whose computational cost limits large-scale applications including dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning. This study proposes the Accident Binary-Continuous Transformer (ABC-Transformer), a decoder-only surrogate combining causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling. It jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and severe accident management guideline (SAMG) states, enabling 5-minute-resolution forecasting over 72-hour transients. Trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000, it achieved lower one-step teacher-forcing error than CNN and recurrent baselines at fine resolutions. Autoregressive reliability was characterized as a full per-scenario distribution over 1100 held-out scenarios. For scheduled-sampling (SS) training, the median $R^2$ is $0.947 \pm 0.006$ and $3.8 \pm 1.0$% of scenarios fail ($R^2<0$; mean $\pm$ SD over four training seeds), while errors accumulate with rollout length. A Mahalanobis self-distance computed from each surrogate rollout, before comparison with the MAAP reference, ranks these failures (ROC-AUC 0.895, reference seed). A threshold at the 40th percentile of calibration scores accepts $36.8 \pm 0.5$% of 550 evaluation scenarios, with no accepted rollout below $R^2 = 0$ for any seed, and routes the rest to MAAP.

papers.title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
papers.abstract: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

papers.title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

papers.title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
papers.abstract: A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average. Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

papers.title: A Neural Physics Solver for Richards Equation
papers.abstract: A new approach to discretise and solve Richards equation based on the finite element method (FEM) is presented. The novelty of the approach, called the Neural Physics method, is that it expresses the discretisation as a convolution neural network (CNN) whose weights are predetermined by the integrals of the basis functions in the FEM. The Neural Physics method is physically consistent as it represents a discretisation of the governing equation and can run on CPUs, GPUs and the latest AI accelerators, resulting in an increase in computational speed. The Neural Physics method is demonstrated for two different discretisations of Richards equation, including a multigrid method that is realised through a U-Net architecture. The accuracy and speed of these methods is tested on a problem with a known analytical solution and compared to a standard FEM, and shows that the Neural Physics method is almost an order of magnitude faster than a comparable FEM. Finally, the Neural Physics method is applied to a real-world test case with integrated experimental data and simulates the infiltration of water through a rain garden. This new approach therefore provides a route to efficiently and accurately solve Richards equation for a wide array of hydrological applications.

papers.title: The Market Is the Reward: Design Markets, Not Just Traders for Human-AI Collective Intelligence
papers.abstract: Learning agents are becoming market participants, yet machine learning still treats the market as a fixed environment, although its payoff rule is the reward agents learn from. This position paper argues that financial AI should build HyperMarkets for human-AI collective intelligence, and not only the agents that trade in them: markets whose liquidity provision, information production, outcome determination, and trading rule are performed or adapted by learning agents and designed jointly toward explicit market-level objectives. In a pre-registered simulation with Claude agents trading for principals, joint design raises a market-level objective by 79% over separately tuned functions, through a trading rule that helps only when slow traders are present, and how evidence is paid for decides whether a stronger agent earns more for its principal. We state when fixed rules or non-market aggregation should be preferred and what findings would refute the case.

papers.title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects
papers.abstract: AI agents can automate software engineering because a compiler or a test suite checks that the code does what the user or the agent intended. In engineering analysis, however, the steps that precede the computation have few easily verifiable checks: modeling a design or an object, deciding how it is used, where supports and loads are applied, and what material each part is made of. A human expert therefore makes these decisions, carries out the steps, and judges the result, one object at a time. We present MechFoundry, an agentic loop coupled with bespoke software that automates structural analyses of real-world objects without a human in the loop. From an object's lexical description, it generates a shape, poses a loading case relevant to how the object is used, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response, and improves the design against the loads it carries. A differentiable GPU solver built on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface enables the transition from shape generation to simulation and optimization. Across 50 everyday and engineering objects, the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average. Without a test suite to check against, we had language-model reviewers grade each session, as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.

papers.title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
papers.abstract: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

papers.title: Nonlinear homogenization of periodic unit cells composed of mixed continuum and structural elements with variationally consistent boundary-member reduction
papers.abstract: Periodic architected materials may be represented by representative volume elements (RVEs) combining continuum, truss, beam, and shell constituents. Their mixed translational and rotational kinematics complicate a consistent scale transition to a macroscale Cauchy continuum. We establish a nonlinear first-order computational homogenization framework for such mixed-dimensional RVEs. An auxiliary finite-strain Cosserat continuum serves solely as a power-equivalent carrier of their virtual power and generalized boundary kinematics. Its uniform rotation is identified with the macroscopic polar rotation and its wryness vanishes, so the effective medium remains of Cauchy type. Under periodic translational and rotational constraints, the Hill-Mandel condition yields a common nodal-force virial for the effective first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, independent of element type. For lower-dimensional members on periodically identified cell boundaries, fractional ownership of internal virtual work is shown to be variationally equivalent to a topology-preserving reduction retaining one representative of each set of periodic element copies. Because this equivalence covers the complete element virtual work and consistent linearization, it applies to geometrically and materially nonlinear and path-dependent constituents without rescaling section properties, constitutive parameters, or internal variables. Numerical examples recover the analytical small-strain response and cubic symmetry of a mixed continuum-shell-beam cell, verify the reduction and discrete power balance, and demonstrate finite-rotation buckling of a hyperelastic Octet lattice and history-dependent yield-surface evolution of an elastoplastic sandwich cell. The open-source implementation abqhom couples the framework to Abaqus.

papers.title: Selecting and verifying load-bearing periodic cells for elastic-wave band gaps with numerical acceptance checks
papers.abstract: A lattice mount must be stiff enough to support equipment and block vibration over a specified frequency range. Fast simulations help rank designs, but their errors can lead to a wrong acceptance decision. We present AMM (AgenticMetamaterials), an open-source Python tool that searches repeating cubic cells for targets on stiffness, the fraction of the cell that is solid, and band gaps. A complete band gap is an interval with no elastic-wave propagation in any direction. A separate checker allows for changes as the simulation grid gets finer. For gaps, it also tests for modes at sampled wave directions and wavelengths, so it can miss modes between samples. In 1,500 near-threshold tests of stiffness and solid fraction, the checker accepted 454 of 750 claims supported by the reference and none of the 750 false claims. Using the finest grid estimate alone accepted 42 false claims. In an independent finite-element comparison on ten new cells built from cubes joined by bars, the checker accepted one of two true gap claims and left all 17 false claims undecided. The reference could not classify the remaining claim. The protocol required every reported edge to err on the side of a narrower gap. The checker failed this test when it placed one upper edge too high, even though it left that thin-bar cell's claim undecided. Separating search from acceptance shows which targets the evidence supports and where a calculation needs further refinement.

papers.title: SciSelect-Gym: An Environment and Benchmark for Active Learning and Bayesian Optimization Configuration Selection
papers.abstract: In many scientific tasks, scientists repeatedly choose a small set of candidates to test, learn from the results, and use the observations to guide the next selection. Methods based on active learning~(AL) or Bayesian optimization~(BO) have been proposed for these iterative screening campaigns with a surrogate model. Yet, selecting the surrogate model and acquisition function for a new dataset remains challenging due to limited empirical evidence, while the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) in making such decisions remains unclear. To address these gaps, we introduce SciSelect-Gym, an environment for simulating AL/BO data selection campaigns and evaluating configuration choices. We conducted simulations of AL/BO data selection campaigns across several settings and more than 100 molecular datasets. Using completed simulation campaigns as context improves LLM recommendation shortlists on held-out datasets more consistently than it improves the quality of their first choice. SciSelect-Gym provides a simulation platform and recommendation protocols for learning how to choose configurations before an acquisition campaign. An implemented agent use case connects these campaign records and simulation tools to LLM-generated configuration-selection policies. The code is provided as supplementary material.

papers.title: The Distributed Run Manager A C++ Library for Distributed Processing
papers.abstract: The DistributedRunManager (DRM) is a C++ library for distributing a computing task among a number of computer systems for parallel processing on a network. The library was originally designed to accelerate synthetic image production for tomographic images, but is also a general solution for distributing a software task across diverse, multiple hardware platforms. The DRM self-configures using a novel C++ class, the ElectionManager. This class selects a server cooperatively at runtime and eliminates the need for a priori distribution configuration. All communication, logging, and fault-tolerance mechanisms are encapsulated by the DRM, providing a "black-box" interface to the application developer.

papers.title: Modeling the Travel Time-Pollution Exposure Trade-off in Urban Route Choice
papers.abstract: Traffic-related air pollution is a major contributor to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and travel time disproportionately drives daily exposure. Conventional routing algorithms minimize time or distance, ignoring street-level pollutant variability and leaving travelers exposed to avoidable risk. We develop a bi-objective routing framework that couples a high-resolution AERMOD-based PM2.5 dispersion surface with a shortest-path algorithm. The algorithm uses a deterministic, gradient-based weight-update scheme to enumerate Pareto-optimal paths along the time-exposure frontier. We apply the framework to 790,000 origin-destination pairs on New York City's road network, covering 1.48 million daily commuters. Link-level concentrations differed by a factor of two or more between adjacent parallel streets. Exposure-aware routes reduced cumulative exposure by about 38% at a median travel time increase of about 28%. The algorithm ran in 30 milliseconds per query and recovered more frontier paths than uniform weight sampling (4.5 vs. 2.4). These results show that exposure-aware routing is computationally practical at metropolitan scale and suitable for real-time navigation and infrastructure planning.

papers.title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
papers.abstract: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.

papers.title: Optimal Seat Movement Strategies Among Modular Bus Units
papers.abstract: Movable seats enable passengers to transfer between coupled modular bus units while remaining seated, but require physical reconfiguration that existing modular transit models largely abstract away. We model seat reconfiguration as a colored generalized sliding-tile puzzle on the physical track graph, capturing simultaneous movements, seat indistinguishability within destination groups, and vertex, edge, and corner-following conflicts. A lexicographic objective minimizes makespan first and then the sum of costs (SoC), which penalizes movements and waiting at non-target positions. We develop an exact time-expanded mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a Boundary-Sequence Dynamic Programming (BSDP) algorithm. BSDP decomposes the problem at single-edge module interfaces and coordinates local schedules through compressed boundary-crossing sequences, provably preserving feasibility and optimal costs. On two- and three-module benchmarks, BSDP achieves mean per-instance speedups of 3.24x and 6.30x over Gurobi, respectively. In fixed-horizon tests with four to seven modules, both methods start from identical greedy schedules and receive a 300 s budget. BSDP obtains lower final SoC than Gurobi on 197 of 200 instances and ties on three, reducing mean final SoC by 17.93%-69.07% across the four size classes. Geometry sensitivity and ablation studies further clarify the contribution of boundary compression to computational performance. The framework links seat reconfiguration to the timing and operational cost of modular bus decoupling.

papers.title: Transverse impact of a Hertzian sphere with an infinite Rayleigh beam
papers.abstract: We study the impact of a Hertzian sphere on an infinite Rayleigh beam, which presents both interesting possibilities for numerical approximation as well as new insights in the multiple-contact-event regime. Here, Galerkin projection using an abstract continuous variable replaces the history-dependent convolution in the impact equations by a system of local-in-time ordinary differential equations. The corresponding approximate solutions are validated against direct numerical solution of the convolution-based formulation and show agreement. Unlike the corresponding Euler-Bernoulli beam impact problem, which is governed by a single nondimensional parameter, the Rayleigh beam impact dynamics is governed by two nondimensional parameters. A parametric study reveals three distinct impact regimes: one regime with a single contact followed by permanent separation, a second regime with a single contact that is sustained thereafter, and an intervening regime with initial separation followed by multiple contact events with diminishing amplitudes, leading eventually to sustained contact. Short- and long-time asymptotic analyses are used to characterize the boundaries between the permanent separation and the re-contact regimes in different parameter regimes. The three significant new aspects of this paper are the system itself (Rayleigh beam instead of Euler Bernoulli beam), the model order reduction achieved through Galerkin projection in an abstract domain, and the detailed parametric study leading to a simple qualitative picture of possible behaviours.

papers.title: A hierarchical graph neural network for efficient particle-resolved prediction of granular flow dynamics
papers.abstract: Graph neural surrogates for granular flow can resolve the motion of individual grains, but propagating information across a large amount of grains requires repeated, costly updates on the full particle graph. This study introduce a Hierarchical Coarse-Grained Graph Neural Network (HCG-GNN) that couples direct interactions between neighboring grains with information exchange on two coarser graphs of occupied spatial cells. In discrete element method (DEM) benchmarks of granular flows down incline planes, HCG-GNN captured key flow characteristics, including front propagation, lateral spreading, deposition morphology, free surface evolution, internal shear behavior, and energy conversion. Results also show that preserving grain-specific features as coarse information returned to the particle graph and integrating predicted accelerations to advance particle motion both improved multi-step accuracy. With 5 of its 7 message-passing steps performed on coarse graphs, HCG-GNN achieved accuracy comparable to a conventional particle-level GNN with a 6.47-fold training speedup and 46.2% lower GPU memory use. A model trained on up to 5000 grains predicted a 2 s release of 10000 grains in 31 s, compared with 2000 s for DEM under the benchmark conditions. This combination of speed and grain-scale resolution supports particle-resolved inverse design, with prescribed runout or discharge targets guiding the search for suitable geometries and grain dynamics revealing the basis for differences in performance.

papers.title: JOINTS: Classification and analytical evaluation of detachable dry connections for reusable concrete elements
papers.abstract: This paper presents a systematic classification for detachable dry joints suitable for the structural reuse of reinforced concrete elements, together with an analytical evaluation of representative configurations. The classification, named JOINTS and applicable to concrete connections beyond the reuse context, organizes the design space along five categories whose initials spell JOINT: the Juxtaposition (spatial arrangement of the paired elements), the Origin (their prior structural function), the Interface geometry, the Newly introduced materials at the joint, and the force-Transfer mechanism. A sixth category, the Score, completes the acronym and evaluates each configuration for sustainability, cost-efficiency, and mechanical performance. From this design space, three representative configurations are evaluated analytically under active post-tensioning, differing in both their joint geometry (planar, stepped, and angled) and their tendon inclination. The evaluation covers failure of the anchorage of the post-tensioning member, the contact limit of the interface, and the material limit of the concrete adjacent to the interface. Although complex joint geometries theoretically enhance interlocking, their benefit is limited by the compressive-shear strength of the concrete. The reinforcement of the reused elements may be damaged near the cut, and the splitting reinforcement that a conventional design would require is not guaranteed to exist. The present analysis therefore conservatively assumes that the concrete at the joint face alone resists the combined compression and shear, neglecting any residual contribution from the existing reinforcement. This analytical evaluation represents a first step toward quantifying the score over a parametric range of connections, here focusing on the mechanical criterion.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Smoothing Selection for Noisy Scattered Surface Reconstruction: Evidence from Synthetic Benchmarks and Water Quality Data
papers.abstract: Sampling geometry may influence both reconstruction stability and the smoothing needed to control noise. This study distinguishes geometry-dependent failure of exact multiquadric radial basis function (RBF) interpolation from variation in validation-selected smoothing. A synthetic benchmark crossed four response families, four 16-point geometries, three slice levels, five observation regimes, and 24 repeated holdouts, yielding 17,280 method-level evaluations. Clough--Tocher cubic interpolation, exact RBF, and smoothed RBF were compared, followed by a Water Quality Portal pilot with 1,950 complete activities. On the synthetic shared-valid domain, exact RBF achieved the lowest noise-free mean RMSE (0.0206), whereas smoothed RBF performed best under noise (0.1807 versus 0.2414 for cubic and 0.6106 for exact RBF). Clustered-gap support produced the largest noisy exact-RBF RMSE (1.2706). Geometry added little explanatory power for log-transformed smoothing: the combined model had $R^2=0.4259$, compared with 0.4096 for noise alone. Reported failure-regression results suggest a stronger geometry signal, but remain unverified without their original model specification. In the environmental pilot, smoothed RBF achieved mean RMSE 0.9877 with no negative-$R^2$ failures. Conflicting responses at identical predictor coordinates made exact interpolation unsuitable. All environmental smoothed-RBF fits selected the largest candidate, preventing geometry--smoothing correlation analysis. The findings motivate geometry-aware failure screening but do not establish a transferable rule for smoothing magnitude. Independent multisite validation, appropriate coordinate scaling, joint scale--smoothing tuning, and conditioning diagnostics are needed before an adaptive policy can be claimed.

papers.title: Credal Wrapper for Uncertainty Modelling in Sparse Geological Data
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for mineral exploration are trained on a few hundred sparse, expensive samples and used to decide where to drill next, so their epistemic uncertainty (EU), the part that more data could remove, matters as much as their predictions. Yet EU cannot be measured on real data, because the counterfactual that defines it is never observed, so estimators are graded by proxies such as out-of-distribution detection and calibration. We contribute a general simulation protocol that makes EU directly computable for a given model and can grade any EU estimator. It separates two estimands the literature conflates, reducible error and estimator spread, builds an oracle reference for each in a synthetic prospectivity field sampled by clustered drilling surveys, and compares uncertainty measures of an identical ensemble within each simulated world. We use it to ask when credal (imprecise-probability) measures are more faithful than Bayesian model averaging (BMA) in the sparse, low-class regime of geological classification. The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when members are few, confirming the small-ensemble advantage reported for credal wrappers; the advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. Secondly, the choice of credal functional matters more than the choice between credal and BMA. Lastly, the credal advantage does not widen as training data are thinned, so it compensates for few posterior samples rather than few data. On real drill-hole geochemistry from South Australia, a resampling oracle reproduces the first finding. The protocol applies to any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

papers.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
papers.abstract: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

papers.title: Large Payments Model
papers.abstract: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. Realizing this shared capability requires handling heterogeneous transaction fields, high-cardinality identifiers, lifecycle-dependent attributes, long histories, and rare outcomes while meeting latency and cost constraints. We present Large Payments Model (LPM), a domain-specific foundation model designed for operational use and trained from scratch on large-scale structured transaction data to learn reusable representations for payment prediction tasks. LPM employs field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision in two complementary architectures: the Independent variant uses hybrid masking and supports efficient per-transaction inference, while the Sequence variant incorporates entity-linked histories through compact latent representations for richer temporal context. Optional distillation enables resource-constrained deployment. We pretrain LPM on up to 400 billion tokens and study scaling, downstream performance, and representation reuse. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services, demonstrating applicability in distinct payment domains. Its representations also facilitate adaptation to a target not observed during pretraining through compact task-specific components. Together with production deployment, these results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

papers.title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
papers.abstract: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $\kappa$ has sharp order $\kappa^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

papers.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
papers.abstract: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

papers.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

papers.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
papers.abstract: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.
